Dwelling, then, entails more than existing and subsisting; it extends beyond simply doing what we need to do-working, socializing, building-to survive to include the richness that is developed and pursued in how we are doing so. Building is not just construction, notjust technics. Nor is it isolable, except at cost, from ambient concerns. To understand place in terms of building necessitates the fullest possible understanding of what makes a location a location. As Heidegger goes on to explain, the fourfold is already wrought with the building of the farmhouse, since the building ofit, which sprang from dwelling, is already a located response to and a living with the fourfold. The farmhouse is built from and sustained by what the earth gives

and lies nestled in the earth's hollows; it receives its direction and temporality from the sky and is further sustained by what the sky brings; the divinities are traced in thankfulness and respect, fear and hope; and death and birth and all the cares of mortals are knit into the house and responsive to the other three aspects of the fourfold, as each of the others similarly join together. None of these things is present in any simple and direct manner. but they can all be seen as gathered in the way of life that gave rise to the farmhouse. Thus, the fourfold cannot be reduced to direct presence, as it is also what remains concealed, although we too often take the mundane persistence of presence as all there is, since it is most near to our everyday concerns. Place is never given in its entirety.

But here we come to the crucial point. This withdrawing is also a form of supporting; it is the repletion of all that is, which in turn ensures that the world is always more than what we make ofit. If the world is to make claims ,on us, ifwe are to dwell in such manner as to attune ourselves to what is noninstrumental. nonrepresentational, then this withdrawal becomes es- :sential. In other words, human knowledge is al ways only partial, and rather tha1\ see this as an invitation to extend knowledge further, as ifwe could pry open all mystery and have it stand revealed before us, Heidegger argues that what remains unconcealed is itself valuable. Dwelling makes being's concealment an occasion for joy and humbleness, thought and insight, guidance and action. It grants the world a kind of meaning or value that, while it cannot speak directly (and hence is neither meaning nor value, exactly), nevertheless calls us in its holding sway and conditions every aspect of our being together. This is the productive "acknowledgment of what is not human in the context of what is" (Thiele, Timely 179). Thus, a location is inseparable from its unique expanse and its ecological connectedness to larger surroundings; all take part in making place a place. I will explore this idea further in the next chapter.

To take one instance, speakers or writers may well understand themselves as working with conscious intent, yet the intention may be causally irrelevant to the effects produced in the audience. Rhetorical theory tends to assume that intent equals result: a rhetor wants to persuade a group of people to vote a certain way, the rhetor succeeds, and therefore the rhetor's intent is held to have been successfully realized through his or her rhetorical art. Arabella Lyon remarks that rhetoric has maintained its boundaries by this adherence to discourse understood as instrumental (4). This is also rhetoric's built-in retroactivity, according to which what works is always telegraphed by an initial intentional action. Curiously, however, intent is rarely called into question when a rhetorical message goes awry; rather, the issue becomes a matter of technique. This idea underpins the longstanding idea of rhetoric as a teachable art. Failure results because one's message was not sufficient for the intent, because one was unprepared for the pa rticular audience, because one made a mistake, and so on. There is no leeway for accidental persuasion, for persuasion at odds with or in spite of intent or even the artistry of rhetorical work. Instead, the causality of rhetorical intent actualized through rhetorical work is often assumed as an unquestionable given. A great deal of excellent work, however, has been done on aleatory methods (see Vitanza, "From Heuristic"); unconscious forms of persuasion, such as Burke's identification, taken from psychoanalysis (see D. Davis, Inessential; Lundberg and Gunn); complexity and ecology (Cooper, Dobrin, Edbauer, Hawk, Lanham); and various proponents of hermeneutic and postmodern thought (Biesecker; Hyde; Lyon; Mailloux, "Rhetorical Hermeneutics" and "Rhetorical Hermeneutics Still"). It is

thus perhaps surprising that we have not made more progress here. But as Lyon suggests, intent has in fact been woefully undertheorized in rhetoric precisely because it is always assumed (3-4). What I have described as essential to an ambient rhetoric-its embodied and embedded or situated character, its dispersal across things that themselves have gradations of agency, and its dynamic emergence within an environment that occasions certain effects-suggests that intent is only one element in a large array of things, feelings, peoples, and forces all complexly interacting. To say this is not to deny the existence or importance of intent but rather to insist that within any given rhetorical event, intent cannot suffice for its full accounting as rhetoric-not to mention the near dogmatic assertion of intent as the expression of the subjective will.

The emphasis on self-consciousness, another aspect of Cole's definition, is just as problematic. Each of the four strands of thought I brought to the notion of ambient rhetoric emphasizes the idea that at any given time, we are only partially conscious of what we are doing, why we are doing it, and what will result from it. When we tether intent to self-consciousness, we cut off large swaths of human activity from rhetorical practice in our rhetorical theory. That last prepositional phrase is crucial: the point is not that what is denied to self-consciousness fails to come into play in rhetorical engagement but that we deny inquiry into those aspects when our rhetorical theory opens itself only onto what is immediately self-conscious and thus easily tethered to humanist notions of willing. Intent and selfconsciousness no doubt matter enormously, but they no longer suffice to determine what rhetoric is and is not. Behind the conventional notion of intention lies a model of human being as an autonomous, self-knowing, subjective agent. Everything I have here described works to undo and disperse this model as a reduced view of human being.

In sum, I hope this book helps us to see such narrowing as a way to impoverish rhetoric when we should be opening it up, not to make it bigger, but to attune us, in rhetoric and via rhetoric, to its fullest flowering. Rhetoric's timeliness as a field of inquiry and a practice has never been more propitious. As I suggested previously, transformations in ourselves, in our historical conjuncture, and in our built environments have occasioned revised understandings of human being and the world. The dynamically ecological imbrications of places, things, and informatics can be read as a (partial) rhetoricization of the world in the most concrete and material way imaginable. Many have read Heidegger's remarks on our relations to things as saying that human beings are immersed in the world through language and everyday practices. This perspective suggests, on the one hand, that we cannot break through or extricate ourselves from our emplacement so as to get at things from the "outside," as it were, and, on the other hand, that the things of the world are never trumped by language or ideas. Our holistic entanglements are material and practical first and foremost. Hubert Dreyfus is a well-known proponent of this position and posits Heidegger as a "robust realist," meaning that Heidegger avoids the Scylla ofnaive realism and the Charybdis of idealism ("Coping" n.p.). The world is a participant in the ongoing event of human being-in-the-world, not a stage or backdrop to what human beings do and say. And this is a nuanced participation, with things emerging from and participating in human practices, and human practices in turn requiring things. Such an interpretation is fine as a first take, except that it exhibits a certain skewing: the nexus remains tethered to human being. Human usage and behavior become the privileged means of access to the background, and things, such as tools, light up to our awareness as we use them; then, when our attention shifts elsewhere, they dim back into the shadowy realm of equipment (Zeug) in general, the undifferentiated, always receding backdrop of"stuff."1 Heidegger certainly lends himself to such a reading. Speaking ofa room, he remarks that we encounter it not as a geometrical space but as "equipment for residingp that we have at least discovered, and that discovery and our activities yield

an arrangement that allows individual items to show themselves (BT 98). I take the steps downstairs into the basement, set out my books, organize my papers, boot the laptop, put some Klaus Schulze on the turntable, sit on the chair at the desk, insert the pen drive, enter words into the chapter file (i.e., write), read, take notes, edit, save the file, put on some Dexter Gordon. adjust the stereo volume, and so forth, with aspects of the room now near and now far from my attentions and activities. In various ways, these things all go together; there is an arrangement from which individual entities already derive their place wherefrom I can weave them through my activities. Entities in turn show up and dim back into the recesses as my attention flows variously through my purposeful activity.

In Tool-Being Graham Harman argues that such readings, reminiscent of Dreyfus, are not wrong but nevertheless miss something crucial to the nature of equipment and objects. Objects can no more be positioned solely within the horizon of human intention or awareness than language can. My example of the basement illustrates this tendency, since everything has its "nearness" and "farness" in relation to my attentions and intentions. One could of course add more history here and pile on thick description across the attentions and intentions of other people, social roles, and equipment. But none of this suffices to give us any ultimate grip on the object. Harman argues that "ifwe could total up all the 'contexts, roles, and social goals' in which a specific bridge or flagpole are currently embedded, this would still not give us the being of these objects" (TB 124). Any use or meaning that I or anyone else can bring, or even the plenitude of people, uses, contexts, histories, and other objects that could be brought forward, only serves to present some particular qualities out of the object's fulsomeness, or what Harman calls its "grand, dark abundance" (TB 125). Indeed. as the new wave of cognitive science (such as the work of Andy Clark, Paul Dourish, Anthony Chemero, and so on) demonstrates, the use of tools and local environmental scaffolding inspires changes in our sense of embodiment, blurring boundaries; to use a computer mouse, for instance, amounts to making that mouse part of one's body, and in so doing, it effectively disappears.8 Thus, predicating ontological distinctions on human attention and its shifting cognitive and bodily boundaries is fruitless; the ontological has to manifest beyond such human-derived loci, and thus withdrawal does not depend on human perception or any other singular interaction.

Empedocles and Heidegger continually emphasized the need to forge a positive way forward, to work not just with who people are but with where they are. We cannot escape the infrastructures, industries, and lifeways people currently have but must work within and through them towards a more ecologically attuned dwelling. In this regard, science, technology, and capitalism will need to become part of that path, despite the fact that these are some of the most common targets for environmentalist critique. On these points I take inspiration from Peter Sloterdijk's digression on spaceships in his massive philosophical trilogy, Spheres. Sloterdijk argues that spaceships are more than technological objects—they are equally ontological interventions. The suturing

of a thing to ontology harkens back to Heidegger, and we can see how Sloterdijk's spaceship updates Heidegger's jugs and bridges. But there is also an inversion: jugs and bridges evoke an interconnected whole to which we are all wedded and indebted; a spaceship, however, operates in a realm of extreme inhospitality. Space is nonconductive for nearly all life as we know it. Since no aspect of dwelling in space can be taken for granted, a spaceship "constitutes a world model," a kind of "immanence machine."73 The level of explicatory detail necessary for surviving in such a harsh environment is vertiginous. To give one small example: astronauts must sleep with fans next to them, less their exhalations, which do not move in zero gravity, suffocate them in a bubble of nitrogen and carbon dioxide.74 There is no resting on unexplicated assumptions, as is possible back on Earth where the ecological background can simply be assumed, as Moore exemplifed through capitalism's cavalier appropriations of nature. Space lacks such "ontological comfort."75

The point, Sloterdijk argues, is that "space travel amounts to an ontological alphabetization: what follows from it is that the elements of being-in-the-world can, and must, be written."76 Sloterdijk picks up the thread we saw connecting Empedocles and Aristotle in the movement from roots to elements, where increasing abstraction and alphabetization formalize as science and episteme. Sloterdijk also counters Abram's argument that abstraction goes hand in hand with the West's loss of intimacy with the environment. Rather, Sloterdijk taps a great affrmation resonant with Empedocles and Heidegger. It is the affrmation of the fourfold. The lesson is that abstraction and alphabetization also gather the fourfold and disclose the worldly depths of rich interconnection. Spaceships necessitate this insight. For life to maintain itself in space, bubbles of lifeworld must be constructed. To construct a bubble of lifeworld requires a profoundly rich explication of an ecological background we take for granted on earth, where our lifeworld is simply given. For spacecraft, these ABCs of lifeworlding must be spelled out and implemented through the technics of disclosure and building. As Heidegger has argued, to build is to dwell, and here we see how this manifests in even the most focused technological enterprise.77

The explicative disclosure necessary for space travel thus affrms some of environmentalism's biggest demons—abstraction, science, technology, capitalist progress. But this disclosive work pushes through their dangers and lights up their roles in the ecological lifeworld it is claimed they despoil. Still, it may be argued that space travel is a feeting pursuit

In an ultimate dialectic, the terms so lead into one another that the completion of each order leads to the next. Thus, a body of positive terms must be brought to a head in a titular term which represents the principle or idea behind the positive terminology as a whole. This summarizing term is in a different order of vocabulary. And if such titles, having been brought into dialectical commerce with one an­ other, are given an order among themselves, there must be a principle of principles involved in such a design—and the step from principles to a principle of principles is likewise both the fulfillment of the pre­ vious order and the transcending of it. We thought of calling the ultimate order “mystical” because the mystic invariably aims to encompass conflicting orders of motivation, not by oudawing any order, however “inferior,” but by finding a place for it in a developmental series. Thus at moments when a mystic vocabulary is most accurate, we should not expect to find a flat antithesis between “body” and “spirit.” Rather, we should ex­ pect “body” (in even its “lowliest” forms) to be treated as a way into 
“spirit.” Since antithesis is so strong a verbal instrument in both rhetoric and dialectic, we may often find “short cuts” where the ex­ tremes of a developmental series are presented as harshly antithetical. But we should not judge by this alone. Rather, look into the writings of any mystic who has left a record of his methods, and you will find that the entry to ultimate communion is made through body, nature, image, systematically treated as a necessary disciplinary step. Indeed, so thoroughly is this the case, that for the most ultimate of his experi­ ences, the mystic will again employ the terms of body, nature, image (on the assumption that, if one has gone through the proper series of steps, one knows how to discount the inadequacies of such language, while the clash of images by oxymoron comes closest to expressing the experience for someone who has not been through it).

Ultimate Elements in the Marxist Persuasion

And since any moment, here and now, would thus represent a developmental principle transcend­ ing the concrete particularity of any one moment in the series, here would be a kind of mystical unity, a oneness that both is and is not, as with the paradox of substance discussed in the Grammar. Be that as it may, I think we may now realize the Grammatical opportunities and embarrassments we encounter as we arrive in our Kantian system at a transcendent realm composed of things-in-themselves. Whatever it may be cosmologically, a thing in itself is Grammatically a thing without reference to context. And for our purposes, that is as far as we need go. Grammatically, then, the transcendent realm is a realm of things-without-context, or things-without-relation.

What does that give us? First, note that relations are "determinations." They assign borders (termini) to a thing. A synonym is "conditions," since "conditions" are likewise contextual, as with the conditions of an organism's existence. Without worrying greatly what it may mean in the literal sense, but merely considering the Grammatical resources available here, let us note that, as the empirical realm is the realm of the determined or conditioned^ and the transcendental realm is the realm of the conditions that provided the terms (determinations), so the transcendent realm of things-in-themselves would be the realm of the undetermined or unconditioned. Whereupon, lo! we find ourselves in a realm of freedomI And so, we have come upon a scene that allows for the possibility of action.

The transcendental had transcended the empirical; it had raised us to a level of generalization that "necessarily" unified the world of particulars, infusing the world of particulars with its spirit. And so now in turn the transcendent has transcended the transcendental, thereby infusing the world of determinism with the spirit of freedom (which is another way of saying that we have added to the world of physical motion the possibilities of moral action).

However, since we began our enterprise with all respect for the requirements of empirical science, we have defined knowledge by pirical tests. Knowledge by definition, then, is the knowledge of ditions and relations. It is the knowledge of appearances, the knowledge of objects as they necessarily appear when seen in terms of our human categories (the categories of the mind in general). So, by defiemcon-

nition, the transcendent realm of the unconditoned things-in-themselves (the scene that contains the possibilities of freedom) cannot be known. Hence, we must restrict the claims we can make about it. But whereas it can't be known, it can be thought about, for we are now thinking about it.

Modern positivists would question whether this statement has meaning; it is certainly "non-sense" if we interpret that word literally, for it is a statement about a realm outside the realm of sensory experience. But if you consider it purely from the standpoint of Grammatical resources, it is obvious that a word as highly generalized as "the conditioned" leaves us with "the unconditioned" as its dialectical opposite, hence as the only term left to be the ground or context of the conditioned. And though we certainly cannot \now this ground, in the scientific meaning which we have given to "knowledge," we can "think" it in recognizing that, so far as the patterns of human thought are concerned, the only term that could antithetically match the "conditioned" would be the "unconditioned." And the unknown to which we thus refer in so basic a pattern of human thought might be characterized as "thought of."

It is an important spot to haggle over, however, if you are going to haggle at all. For once you let this point go by unquestioned, you give Kant some important advantages. If this realm of the things-inthemselves can be thought though not known, this limitation upon our claims to knowledge about them applies in reverse to science. Science compels us to admit that things-in-themselves can't be known; but in putting them outside the area of scientific knowledge, by the same token we put them outside the area of scientific refutation or denial. The sources of morality thus lie beyond the reach of the terms proper to the physical sciences (which is but another way of saying that, in this terminology, action cannot be reduced to motion). In his preface to the second edition Kant said: "I must abolish knou;ledge, to make room for belief " In taking the action out of the scene which he equated with knowledge, he had to make sure that there was still room for an act of faith.
